PocketPlay X3 Teardown

Written By: Sam Okafor
  • Comments26

Difficulty

Difficult

Steps

12

Time Required

2 hours

Introduction

The PocketPlay X3 is a handheld game console with a 7-inch OLED screen, detachable controllers on rails and a dock for the television. We bought one on launch day and took it apart to see how it is built and how easy it will be to repair: whether the battery can be changed without heat, whether the joysticks, which wore out quickly on the last model, are now held by screws, whether the screen is glued to the frame, and whether the storage and the fan can be reached without removing the main board. As always we sorted every screw by length and type, measured the battery, and noted each connector, so that anyone who opens their own console later will know what to expect.

Tools

  • Tri-point Y00 Screwdriver

  • Phillips #00 Screwdriver

  • iOpener

  • Opening Picks

  • Spudger

  • Tweezers

  1. Step 1

    • The X3 measures 242 x 102 x 14 mm and weighs 420 g with both controllers attached.

    • Out of the box the console runs a new chip, a larger 64 GB storage and a brighter OLED panel, and the kickstand now runs across the whole width of the back.

  2. Step 2

    • Four tri-point Y00 screws on the back and two Phillips #00 screws on the top edge hold the rear cover.

    • Two more Phillips screws hide under the kickstand, which has to be swung open to reach them.

    • With all eight screws out, the cover lifts away from the bottom edge first, held only by two small clips near the game card slot.

  3. Step 3

    • Under the cover is a metal shield that also acts as a heat spreader, held by seven Phillips screws.

    • A thick graphite sheet on the inside of the shield is stuck to the processor's thermal pad; peel it slowly or it tears.

    • The microSD reader is soldered to the main board on this model, so a broken card slot means a board repair.

  4. Step 4

    • The screen is glued to the plastic frame all the way round with a strong adhesive.

    • We warmed the edges with an iOpener for two minutes, lifted a corner with a suction cup and slid opening picks under it, working round slowly because the OLED panel bends and cracks easily.

    • The display cable runs under the battery, so the screen cannot come off completely until the battery is out.

  5. Step 5

    • Next we lift out the speakers, which sit in rubber cups at each end of the frame and come out with a pull.

    • Their wires run to a single connector near the left rail, which pops off with a spudger.

    • The speakers are the same part on both sides, which should keep replacement costs down.

  6. Step 6

    • The battery is the largest part inside, a 4,310 mAh, 16.6 Wh cell that covers most of the back of the frame.

    • It is held down by two stretch-release adhesive strips with pull tabs at the bottom edge; pull them slowly and flat, and the battery lifts out without heat or prying.

    • This is the biggest improvement over the last model, whose battery was glued down and needed isopropyl alcohol and a lot of patience to free.

    • A small battery connector at the top right is covered by a metal bracket with one Phillips screw.

  7. Step 7

    • With the battery out we can finally free the display cable and lift the screen away.

    • The OLED panel is a single part with its digitizer, so a cracked glass means replacing the whole panel.

  8. Step 8

    • The joystick modules now sit in the rail assemblies and are held by two Phillips screws each, with a short ribbon cable to a ZIF connector on the rail board.

    • Flip up the ZIF connector's black locking flap with a fingernail before pulling the ribbon out, or the connector will break.

    • Fixing joystick drift should be a ten-minute job on the X3, where it needed the whole console taken apart before.

  9. Step 9

    • The cooling fan is held by three screws and has its own small connector; it lifts out together with its copper heat pipe.

    • Dust collects on the fan grille, so a blast of compressed air through the top vent from time to time is worth doing.

  10. Step 10

    • The main board comes out after eleven screws and five more connectors.

    • The processor is a custom eight-core chip, and beside it are 8 GB of LPDDR5 memory in two packages.

    • The Wi-Fi and Bluetooth chip is a Murata module under a small shield of its own near the antenna cables.

  11. Step 11

    • The USB-C port is on its own small board, held by two screws and one cable, so a worn charging port no longer means a new main board.

    • The headphone jack, in contrast, is soldered to the main board.

  12. Step 12

    • Last, the game card reader comes out of the top of the frame, held by two screws, and the volume buttons come out with their small flex cable.

Conclusion

The PocketPlay X3 earns a repairability score of 6 out of 10: the battery, the joysticks, the fan and the charging port can all be replaced with ordinary tools, but the glued OLED screen and the soldered microSD reader and headphone jack will make some repairs expensive.

Written By: Sam Okafor

Introduction

If your walk-behind mower starts and then dies, or will only run with the choke on, old fuel has probably gummed up the carburetor. This guide shows how to take the float bowl off and clean the main jet.

Tools

  • Socket set

  • Flathead screwdriver

  • Carburetor cleaner spray

  • Safety glasses

Parts

  • Float bowl gasket

  1. Step 1

    • Work outdoors, away from flames.

    • Pull the spark plug wire off.

    • Let the engine cool.

  2. Step 2

    • Close the fuel valve.

    • Or run the tank dry first.

    • Tilt the mower air filter up.

  3. Step 3

    • Remove the air filter cover.

    • Lift out the filter.

    • Inspect it; replace if oily.

  4. Step 4

    • Find the float bowl.

    • It hangs under the carburetor.

    • Place a rag below it.

  5. Step 5

    • Undo the 10 mm bowl nut.

    • Catch the fuel in a jar.

    • Fuel is flammable; no smoking.

  6. Step 6

    • Spray cleaner through the jet.

    • Hold it up to the light.

    • The hole must be clear.

    • Never poke it with wire.

  7. Step 7

    • Fit a new bowl gasket.

    • Refit the bowl and nut.

    • Do not overtighten it.

  8. Step 8

    • Refit the filter and cover.

    • Reconnect the spark plug wire.

    • Open the fuel valve and start.

If the mower still surges after cleaning, the carburetor may need a rebuild kit or replacement.

Written By: Sam Okafor

32

Introduction

A mechanical sewing machine runs for decades if the lint is cleaned out and the moving parts are oiled once a year. This guide covers a full service of a typical straight-stitch machine.

Tools

  • Small screwdriver

  • Lint brush

  • Sewing machine oil

  1. Step 1

    • Unplug the machine.

    • Remove the needle and presser foot.

  2. Step 2

    • Open the bobbin cover.

    • Take out the bobbin.

  3. Step 3

    • Remove the two needle plate screws.

    • Lift off the needle plate.

  4. Step 4

    • Lift out the bobbin case.

    • Note how it sits.

  5. Step 5

    • Brush lint from the feed dogs.

    • Use a small stiff brush.

  6. Step 6

    • Brush lint from the hook race.

  7. Step 7

    • Wipe the hook race with a dry cloth.

  8. Step 8

    • Put one drop of sewing machine oil on the hook race.

    • Do not use cooking oil.

  9. Step 9

    • Refit the bobbin case.

    • The notch goes at the top.

  10. Step 10

    • Refit the needle plate.

  11. Step 11

    • Remove the top cover screw.

    • Lift off the top cover.

  12. Step 12

    • Brush lint from the top.

  13. Step 13

    • Oil the needle bar where it slides.

    • One drop is enough.

  14. Step 14

    • Oil the presser bar.

  15. Step 15

    • Refit the top cover.

  16. Step 16

    • Remove the end cover.

    • It slides off to the left.

  17. Step 17

    • Clean the take-up lever area.

  18. Step 18

    • Oil the take-up lever pivot.

  19. Step 19

    • Refit the end cover.

  20. Step 20

    • Tip the machine on its back.

  21. Step 21

    • Remove the base plate screws.

  22. Step 22

    • Clean the lower shaft area.

  23. Step 23

    • Oil each point where a shaft turns in a bushing.

    • Look for small oil holes.

  24. Step 24

    • Turn the handwheel to spread the oil.

  25. Step 25

    • Wipe off any extra oil.

  26. Step 26

    • Refit the base plate.

  27. Step 27

    • Stand the machine upright.

  28. Step 28

    • Check the motor belt tension.

    • It should flex about 6 mm.

  29. Step 29

    • Fit a new needle.

    • Flat side to the back.

  30. Step 30

    • Refit the presser foot.

  31. Step 31

    • Sew on scrap fabric for a minute.

    • This soaks up extra oil.

  32. Step 32

    • Check the stitch.

    • Adjust the top tension if loops form underneath.

Conclusion

Service the machine once a year, or after every big project.

Home Router Power Jack Replacement

Written By: Sam Okafor
  • Comments7

Difficulty

Difficult

Steps

8

Time Required

1 - 2 hours

Introduction

A loose or burnt DC power jack is the most common hardware fault of home routers. This guide replaces the jack on the main board with a soldering iron.

Tools

  • Torx T8 Screwdriver

  • Soldering iron

  • Desoldering braid

  • Spudger

Parts

  • 5.5 x 2.1 mm DC jack

  1. Step 1

    • Power off the router. Unplug the power adapter and all the Ethernet cables, and wait one minute.

    • Write down the network name and password on the label before you start; the label sometimes tears when the case is opened.

  2. Step 2

    • Peel off the four rubber feet. Under them are four Torx T8 screws.

    • Remove the screws and keep them in a cup.

  3. Step 3

    • Insert a spudger in the seam at the back. Twist it to release the clips, then work round the sides.

    • Lift the top half of the case off.

  4. Step 4

    • Disconnect the two antenna cables from the board. They snap straight up.

  5. Step 5

    • Remove the three screws holding the board and lift it out.

    • Look at the old jack: a burnt or melted jack usually means the adapter or the board has been overheating, so check the adapter too.

  6. Step 6

    • Heat each of the three jack pins and remove the solder with desoldering braid. Then rock the old jack out gently.

    • Do not overheat the pads; they can lift off the board.

  7. Step 7

    • Fit the new jack and solder its three pins. Make sure it sits flat on the board.

    • Check with a multimeter that the centre pin is not shorted to the outer sleeve.

  8. Step 8

    • Reassemble in reverse order and test the router with its own adapter.

pages.ifixit/Refrigerator:
Refrigerator

Repair guides and support for household refrigerators and fridge-freezers.

Guides

Refrigerator Door Gasket Replacement

Refrigerator Defrost Thermostat Replacement

Refrigerator Condenser Fan Replacement

Troubleshooting

Fridge is not cooling

First check that the thermostat dial has not been turned down and that the door closes fully on its gasket.

  • Dirty condenser coils: vacuum the coils at the back or underneath the fridge every six months.
  • Failed condenser fan: if the compressor runs but the fan behind it does not turn, replace the fan.
  • Blocked vents: food packed against the vent between the freezer and the fridge stops cold air reaching the fridge.

Water on the floor

A clogged defrost drain is the usual cause. Pour warm water with a little baking soda down the drain hole at the back of the fridge until it runs freely into the pan underneath.

Ice builds up in the freezer

Thick frost on the back wall of the freezer means the automatic defrost has failed: the defrost heater, the defrost thermostat or the timer is at fault.

Defrosting by hand

Step 1

Unplug the fridge and empty the freezer into a cool box.

Step 2

Leave the door open with towels on the floor and a tray under the drain. Never chip the ice with a knife; you can puncture the refrigerant tubes.

Step 3

When all the ice has melted, dry the inside, plug the fridge in and wait four hours before refilling it.
pages.ifixit/Trailcam_R2_Teardown:
Trailcam R2 Teardown

Written By: Sam Okafor
  • Comments3

Difficulty

Moderate

Steps

8

Time Required

45 minutes

Introduction

The Trailcam R2 is a weatherproof wildlife camera that straps to a tree, takes pictures and video when its passive infrared sensor sees a warm animal move, and runs for months on eight AA batteries. Wildlife researchers, farmers and hunters leave these cameras out in rain, frost and summer heat for a whole season, so we wanted to know how well the case is sealed, how the infrared flash is built, whether the lens fogs, and whether the parts that usually fail in the field, the battery contacts, the memory card slot and the latch, can be replaced by the owner. We opened two cameras, one new and one that had spent two winters on a fence post, and compared them part by part.

Tools

  • Phillips #1 Screwdriver

  • Spudger

  • Tweezers

  • Multimeter

  1. Step 1

    • The R2 is 135 x 100 x 75 mm and weighs 290 g without batteries.

    • The front holds the lens, the PIR sensor behind its ribbed plastic window, and a ring of 40 infrared LEDs; the back opens on a hinge with a single latch.

  2. Step 2

    • Six Phillips #1 screws around the back of the front shell hold the two halves together.

    • Under them, a thick foam gasket runs all the way round the seam.

  3. Step 3

    • With the shell open we see the main board, the battery tray and the LED board stacked on top of each other, joined by three cables.

  4. Step 4

    • The battery tray is moulded into the back half and holds eight AA cells in two rows of four, wired as two packs of 6 V in parallel.

    • The contacts are nickel-plated spring steel, and on the old camera two of them were green with corrosion where water had got past the latch.

  5. Step 5

    • The LED board is held by four screws and carries 40 infrared LEDs at 940 nm, which glow so faintly that animals and people cannot see them at night.

  6. Step 6

    • The seal is where this camera has been designed with the most care, and where the old camera shows what happens in the field after two winters.

    • The main seam is closed by a closed-cell foam gasket 6 mm wide, pressed flat by the six screws; on the old camera it had taken a permanent set of about 1 mm but still sealed, and we found no water inside the front shell at all.

    • The latch is the weak point: water ran down the strap, under the latch hook and into the battery compartment, which explains the corroded contacts we saw in the last step.

    • The lens window is sealed with a ring of silicone and has a small sachet of silica gel behind it to stop it fogging; on the old camera the sachet had turned from orange to green, its colour when saturated, and the inside of the window was misted.

    • The PIR window is ultrasonically welded to the shell and cannot leak, but it also cannot be replaced if it cracks.

    • Owners who leave the camera out all year can add a strip of self-amalgamating tape over the latch and replace the silica gel sachet each spring; both are cheap and need no tools.

  7. Step 7

    • The main board comes out after four screws and the three cables.

    • The image sensor is a 5-megapixel part, upscaled in software to the 20 megapixels claimed on the box.

  8. Step 8

    • The SD card slot is soldered to the main board and is a spring-loaded push-push type.

    • It takes cards up to 32 GB; larger cards must be formatted as FAT32 or the camera will not see them.

Conclusion

The Trailcam R2 is simple inside and well sealed at the seam, but a leaky latch and a soldered card slot mean that the commonest field failures are not easily repaired. We give it 5 out of 10.

Laptop L14 SSD Replacement

Written By: Sam Okafor
  • Comments5

Difficulty

Easy

Steps

8

Time Required

15 minutes

Introduction

Replace or upgrade the M.2 solid-state drive in an L14 laptop. You will need to reinstall the operating system on a new, empty drive.

Tools

  • Phillips #0 Screwdriver

  • Spudger

Parts

  • M.2 2280 NVMe SSD

  1. Step 1

    • Shut the laptop down completely. Do not just close the lid; a sleeping laptop can wake up while you work.

    • Unplug the charger and any USB devices.

  2. Step 2

    • Turn the laptop over on a soft cloth. Loosen the nine captive screws on the bottom cover; they stay in the cover.

    • Starting at the hinge, pry the cover off with a spudger. The front clips are the tightest.

  3. Step 3

    • Disconnect the battery. Pull the connector straight back by its tabs, not by the wires.

    • This prevents a short circuit when you remove the drive.

  4. Step 4

    • Find the SSD next to the fan. Remove the single screw at the end of the drive.

    • The drive springs up at an angle of about 20 degrees.

  5. Step 5

    • Pull the drive out of its slot at the same angle. Keep the screw and the thermal pad.

    • Insert the new drive at the same angle until its gold contacts disappear into the slot.

  6. Step 6

    • Press the drive down and refit the screw. Do not overtighten it.

    • Move the thermal pad from the old drive to the new one if the new drive has none.

  7. Step 7

    • Reconnect the battery. Refit the bottom cover, pressing the clips home all the way round.

    • Tighten the nine screws.

  8. Step 8

    • Start the laptop and press F12 to choose a boot device. Install the operating system from a USB stick.

    • If the new drive does not appear, check that it is an NVMe drive; this slot does not take SATA M.2 drives.

Hypothermia

Hypothermia is a body core temperature below 35.0°C (95.0°F). It happens when the body loses heat faster than it makes it, usually from cold air, cold water, wind or wet clothes.[3]

Old people, babies, people who are drunk and people who are injured or exhausted outdoors are most at risk. It can happen above freezing, for example to someone soaked by rain in a wind.[4]

Signs and symptoms

The signs depend on how cold the body has become; they are usually described in three stages.[5]

  • Stage 1: mild hypothermia (32–35°C). Shivering, cold pale skin, fast breathing and clumsy hands.
  • Stage 2: moderate hypothermia (28–32°C). Violent shivering that may stop, slurred speech, confusion and drowsiness.
  • Stage 3: severe hypothermia (below 28°C). No shivering, unconsciousness, a weak slow pulse and slow breathing; the person may look dead.

Some people with severe hypothermia take off their clothes because they feel hot, a sign called paradoxical undressing.[6]

First aid

The first step is to get the person out of the cold and the wind, into shelter if possible, and to call emergency services.[7]

  1. Handle the person gently and keep them lying flat; rough movement can upset the heart rhythm of a very cold person.
  2. Remove wet clothing, cutting it off if needed, and replace it with dry clothes.
  3. Wrap the person in blankets or a sleeping bag, covering the head and neck, with insulation underneath them as well as on top.
  4. If they are fully awake and can swallow, give warm sweet drinks; never give alcohol.
  5. Do not rub the limbs or put the person in a hot bath; warm the trunk first, for example with skin-to-skin contact.
  6. If the person is not breathing normally, start CPR and keep going until help arrives; people have recovered after hours of CPR.

Prevention

Dress in layers, keep dry, cover the head and hands, eat and drink enough, and avoid alcohol in the cold.[8]

Cookbook:Injera

Injera is a sour, spongy flatbread from Ethiopia and Eritrea, made from teff flour and fermented for several days. It is both plate and spoon: stews are served on it and eaten with torn pieces of it.[12]

Ingredients

  • 500 g teff flour
  • 750 ml water, plus more as needed
  • Salt to taste

Procedure

  1. Mix the teff flour and water in a large bowl to a smooth, thin batter, cover it with a cloth and leave it at room temperature.
  2. Leave the batter to ferment for two to four days, until it is bubbly and smells sour; a yellowish liquid on top can be poured off.
  3. Stir in the salt and enough water to make a batter as thin as pancake batter.
  4. Heat a large non-stick pan or a mitad over medium heat without oil.
  5. Pour the batter in a thin spiral from the outside in, then cover the pan as soon as bubbles form all over the surface.
  6. Cook for two to three minutes, without turning, until the edges lift and the top is dry; lift it off onto a cloth to cool.

Notes, tips, and variations

Teff is gluten-free. Where teff is hard to find, a mixture of teff with wheat, barley or sorghum flour is used, but the bread is less sour and less spongy.[13]

Keep a little of the fermented batter to start the next batch; it shortens the fermentation to a day or two.[14]

Beekeeping

This book is an introduction to keeping honey bees for people who have never kept them, written for small-scale and village beekeepers with simple equipment.[15]

Contents

  • Chapter 1: Why keep bees, and what it costs to start
  • Chapter 2: The honey bee colony: queen, workers and drones
  • Chapter 3: Hives: top-bar, Langstroth and log hives
  • Chapter 4: Protective clothing and the smoker
  • Chapter 5: Catching a swarm or buying a colony
  • Chapter 6: Inspecting a hive through the year
  • Chapter 7: Harvesting honey and wax
  • Chapter 8: Pests and diseases

Getting started

The first step is to learn from an experienced beekeeper: join a local association, or spend a season helping someone before buying a hive of your own. Check also that nobody in the household is allergic to bee stings.[16]

Bees need a source of water within a few hundred metres, and flowers for nectar and pollen through as much of the year as possible. Place hives facing the morning sun, sheltered from wind, and away from paths so that the flight line does not cross where people walk.[17]

Stings

Every beekeeper is stung. Scrape the sting out sideways with a fingernail or a card as quickly as possible. Pain and swelling around the sting are normal; swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing or dizziness are signs of a severe allergic reaction that needs emergency medical help.[18]

Outdoor Survival/Desert

This chapter covers staying alive when stranded in a hot desert, by car breakdown or when lost on foot. The rules are simple: stay with the vehicle, keep out of the sun, save sweat, not water, and make yourself easy to find.[19]

Understand

A person resting in the shade at 40°C loses about a litre of sweat a day; walking in the sun can cost a litre an hour. Without water, most people survive only two or three days in desert heat, less if they walk.[20]

Get around

Do not walk unless you know help is close. If you must move, walk at night, at dawn and at dusk, rest in shade during the day, and leave a note at the vehicle saying which way you went.[21]

Drink

Drink the water you have when you are thirsty; rationing water while dehydrated does not make it last longer in the body. Do not drink urine, sea water, alcohol or radiator coolant, which is poisonous. Most cactus sap is not drinkable and causes vomiting.[22]

Eat

Food is far less important than water and digestion uses water, so eat little if water is short. Do not eat lizards, insects or plants you do not know.[23]

Sleep

Desert nights can be cold. Sleep off the ground on a layer of clothing or brush, and keep a fire going if you can; it also signals your position.[24]

Stay safe

Rest in the shade of the vehicle or under a cloth stretched over a hollow, not on the hot ground. Keep the body covered with loose light clothes and a hat; clothes slow sweating. Signal with a mirror, smoke by day and fire by night, and three of anything (fires, whistle blasts) as a distress call.[25]

Chocolate

Chocolate is a food produced from the roasted and ground kernels of the cacao seed, sold as a solid bar, a liquid or a paste, or used to flavour other foods.[26]

Cacao has been eaten in Mesoamerica for at least three thousand years; the Maya and the Aztecs drank it as a bitter, frothy drink. Today more than half of the world's cacao is grown in West Africa, mostly in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana.[27]

History

The earliest evidence of cacao use, residue in pottery from Ecuador, is about 5,300 years old. Spanish conquistadors brought cacao to Europe in the 16th century, where it was drunk sweetened with sugar and spiced with cinnamon.[28]

In 1828 Coenraad van Houten in the Netherlands invented a press that squeezed most of the fat (cocoa butter) out of the roasted beans, leaving cocoa powder. In 1847 the British firm J. S. Fry & Sons made the first solid chocolate bar, and in 1875 Daniel Peter in Switzerland added condensed milk to make the first milk chocolate.[29]

Production

Cacao pods are harvested by hand and split open; the beans and their pulp are left to ferment for five to seven days, which develops the chocolate flavour, and are then dried in the sun.[30]

At the factory the beans are roasted, cracked and winnowed to leave the nibs, which are ground into a thick paste called cocoa liquor (it holds no alcohol). Chocolate is made by mixing cocoa liquor with extra cocoa butter and sugar, then refining the mixture between rollers and stirring it for hours in a conche.[31]

The chocolate is then tempered, heated and cooled to precise temperatures so that the cocoa butter sets in its stable crystal form, which gives a glossy surface and a clean snap.[32]

Types

Dark chocolate is produced by adding fat and sugar to cocoa liquor; in the European Union it must hold at least 35% cocoa solids.[33]

Milk chocolate is sweet chocolate that also contains milk powder or condensed milk; EU rules require at least 25% cocoa solids and 14% dry milk solids.[34]

White chocolate holds no cocoa solids at all, only cocoa butter, sugar and milk solids, which is why it is ivory in colour.[35]

Health

Chocolate contains moderate amounts of caffeine and larger amounts of theobromine, a related stimulant; a 50 g bar of dark chocolate has about as much caffeine as a quarter of a cup of coffee.[36]

Milk chocolate contains large amounts of sugar and saturated fat, and a 100 g bar holds more than 500 kilocalories.[37]

Theobromine is poisonous to dogs and cats, which break it down much more slowly than people; dark chocolate, with the most theobromine, is the most dangerous to them.[38]

Economics

About 5 million tonnes of cacao are grown each year, most of it on small family farms. Chocolate makers buy large amounts of cocoa through traders, and the price has been very volatile since 2023.[39]

Toothpaste is a paste or gel used with a toothbrush to clean the teeth and keep them and the gums healthy.[40]

Most toothpastes sold today contain fluoride, which helps prevent tooth decay, and are used twice a day.[41]

Ingredients

Besides 20–42% water, a toothpaste has three main kinds of ingredient: abrasives, fluoride and detergents.[42]

Abrasives

Abrasives make up at least half of a typical toothpaste. They are fine particles of hydrated silica, calcium carbonate or aluminium hydroxide that scrub off plaque and stains without scratching the enamel.[43]

Fluoride

Fluoride is the active ingredient that protects against decay. It is added as sodium fluoride, stannous fluoride or sodium monofluorophosphate; adult toothpastes usually hold 1,000 to 1,500 parts per million of fluoride.[44]

Detergents and other components

Sodium lauryl sulfate is the usual foaming agent. Humectants such as glycerol and sorbitol stop the paste drying out, thickeners such as carrageenan hold it together, and flavourings, usually mint, and sweeteners such as xylitol make it pleasant to use.[45]

Safety

Toothpaste is safe when used as directed, but it should be spat out, not swallowed. Children who swallow large amounts of toothpaste over years can develop dental fluorosis, white marks on the teeth.[46]

Toothpaste mixed with chalk was once sold for polishing silver, and toothpaste is still used to clean scratched headlights; such uses wear the surface away.[47]

History

The ancient Egyptians cleaned their teeth with a powder of ox hooves, myrrh, burnt eggshells and pumice. Toothpastes made with soap and chalk were sold in jars in the 19th century, and the first toothpaste in a tube appeared in 1892.[48]

Fluoride toothpaste was introduced in the 1950s after studies showed that it reduced decay in children by about a quarter.[49]

Bone

A bone is a rigid organ that forms part of the skeleton of vertebrates. Bones protect the organs of the body, produce red and white blood cells, store minerals, and allow movement.[50]

The adult human skeleton has 206 bones; a baby is born with about 270, some of which fuse as it grows.[51]

Structure

Bone tissue is of two kinds. Compact (cortical) bone forms the hard outer shell and makes up about 80% of the skeleton's mass; spongy (cancellous) bone, a lattice of thin struts, fills the ends of long bones and the inside of the vertebrae.[52]

The bone marrow inside the cavities produces large amounts of blood cells: about 500 billion a day in an adult.[53]

Composition

The bone matrix is about 30% organic material and 70% minerals. The organic part is mostly type I collagen, a protein that gives bone its flexibility; the mineral part is mostly hydroxyapatite, a calcium phosphate crystal that gives it its hardness.[54]

Bones store large amounts of calcium and phosphate and release them into the blood when the body needs them.[55]

Healing

A broken bone heals in stages: a blood clot forms, then a soft callus of cartilage, then a hard callus of woven bone, which is slowly remodelled over months. A simple fracture in an adult takes about six to eight weeks to knit, longer in older people.[56]

Anyone who may have a broken bone should keep the limb still and get medical help; a bone that has broken through the skin needs emergency care because of the risk of infection.[57]

Disorders

Osteoporosis, a loss of bone mass with age, makes bones fragile; it is most common in women after the menopause. Rickets, a softening of the bones in children, is caused by a lack of vitamin D or calcium.[58]

Pencil

A pencil is a writing or drawing tool with a solid core of pigment inside a protective case, usually of wood, that keeps the core from breaking and from marking the hand.[59]

Pencils make marks by abrasion, leaving a trail of the core on paper, and unlike ink their marks can be rubbed out with an eraser.[60]

History

A large deposit of very pure graphite was found at Borrowdale in Cumbria, England, around 1565. Local people used it to mark sheep, and it was soon sawn into sticks and wrapped in string or wood. People at the time thought it was a kind of lead ore and called it plumbago, which is why the core is still called the lead.[61]

In 1795 Nicolas-Jacques Conté, a French engineer, found that powdered graphite mixed with clay and fired in a kiln made a core as good as pure graphite, and that more clay made a harder pencil.[62]

Manufacture

Today the core of a graphite pencil is a mixture of finely ground graphite and clay, with a little wax, pressed into thin rods and baked at about 1,000°C. The rods are laid in grooves in slats of cedar, a second slat is glued on top, and the sandwich is cut into pencils.[63]

Despite its name, pencil lead holds no lead, and never has. Pencils were once painted with lead paint, but this was banned in many countries in the 20th century.[64]

Grading

The hardness of the core is shown by letters: H for hard, B for black (soft), and HB in between. A 2H pencil is harder than an H, and a 4B is softer and darker than a 2B. Softer pencils have more graphite and less clay.[65]

Other kinds

Coloured pencils have cores of pigment bound with wax or oil instead of graphite. Mechanical pencils push thin leads of polymer and graphite through a metal tip.[66]

Lead poisoning from chewing pencils is a myth, but the paint on very old pencils could contain large amounts of lead.[67]

Lead–acid battery

The lead–acid battery is a rechargeable battery invented in 1859 by the French physicist Gaston Planté. It was the first rechargeable battery and is still the most common kind used to start cars.[68]

Although it stores little energy for its weight, it can deliver large amounts of current for a short time, which is what a starter motor needs, and it is cheap.[69]

Construction

A typical 12 V car battery has six cells in series, each giving about 2.1 V. Each cell holds a stack of plates: negative plates of spongy lead and positive plates of lead dioxide, separated by thin porous sheets, all standing in sulfuric acid diluted with water to about 37%.[70]

The case is moulded polypropylene. In absorbent glass mat (AGM) batteries the acid is soaked into glass-fibre mats instead of being free liquid, so the battery cannot spill.[71]

Charging

While the battery discharges, both plates turn to lead sulfate and the acid becomes weaker; charging reverses this. Overcharging splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, a mixture of gases that can explode, so batteries should be charged in a ventilated place, away from sparks.[72]

Safety

The acid burns skin and eyes. Wear eye protection when working near a battery, and if acid gets on skin or in the eyes, rinse it with plenty of running water and get medical help.[73]

Recycling

Lead–acid batteries are among the most recycled products: in many countries more than 95% of the lead is recovered. The lead is toxic, so old batteries must go to a scrap dealer or recycling point, never into household rubbish.[74]

Mars

Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun. It is a rocky planet about half the size of Earth, with a thin atmosphere and a surface coloured red by iron oxide dust.[75]

Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, and a day only 37 minutes longer than Earth's.[76]

Internal structure

Like Earth, Mars has separated into layers. Seismometer readings from the InSight lander show a liquid core of iron and nickel with a lot of sulfur, about 1,830 km in radius, under a mantle of silicate rock and a crust 24 to 72 km thick, mostly of basalt.[77]

Surface

Olympus Mons, a shield volcano 22 km high, is the largest volcano in the Solar System by volume and by height. Valles Marineris, a system of canyons 4,000 km long, would stretch across the United States.[78]

Mars holds large amounts of water ice in its polar caps and under the ground at middle latitudes; if the ice in the south polar cap melted it would cover the planet to a depth of 11 m.[79]

The fine dust that covers the surface is made of iron oxide and is lifted by planet-wide dust storms that can last for months.[80]

Atmosphere

The Martian atmosphere is about 95% carbon dioxide, 2.8% nitrogen and 2% argon by volume, with traces of oxygen and water vapour. Its pressure at the surface is less than 1% of Earth's.[81]

Exploration

More than fifty spacecraft have been sent to Mars since 1960, and about half have failed. Rovers such as Curiosity and Perseverance have found that liquid water once flowed on the surface.[82]

The decathlon is a combined event in athletics consisting of ten track and field events held over two consecutive days.[83]

Seawater

Seawater is water from a sea or ocean. On average it has a salinity of about 3.5%: every kilogram holds about 35 grams of dissolved salts.[88]

Seawater is denser than fresh water and freezes at about −2°C. Drinking it makes thirst worse, because the kidneys need more water than it holds to remove its salt.[89]

Composition

About 96.5% of seawater by mass is water. Of the dissolved salts, chloride and sodium ions are by far the most common, together about 85%; sulfate, magnesium, calcium and potassium make up most of the rest.[90]

Rivers carry large amounts of dissolved minerals into the sea every year, and the oceans absorb about a quarter of the carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels.[91]

Fresh water can be made from seawater by distillation or by reverse osmosis, in which seawater is forced through a membrane at high pressure. A solar still made with a plastic sheet can produce small amounts of drinking water in an emergency.[92]

pages.wikipedia/Honey:
Honey

Honey is a sweet, thick food made by honey bees and some related insects from the nectar of flowers.[98]

Bees store it in wax combs inside the hive as food for the winter; beekeepers take the surplus.[99]

Production

Forager bees suck nectar from flowers and carry it back in their honey stomachs, where enzymes begin to break its sugar down. In the hive, worker bees pass it from mouth to mouth and fan it with their wings until most of the water has evaporated, then seal it in the comb with a cap of wax.[100]

A strong colony can produce large amounts of honey in a good season, 25 kg or more beyond what it needs for itself.[101]

Composition

Honey is about 80% sugars, mostly fructose (about 38%) and glucose (about 31%), and about 17% water. The rest is maltose and other sugars, acids, minerals and enzymes.[102]

It also contains small amounts of vitamins and antioxidants, but too little to matter in the diet.[103]

Preservation

Because it holds so little water and is acidic, honey does not spoil; pots of edible honey thousands of years old have been found in Egyptian tombs. It may crystallise in the cold, which is harmless; warming the jar in hot water makes it liquid again.[104]

Health

Honey should never be given to babies under one year old, because it can carry spores of the bacterium that causes infant botulism.[105]

People with diabetes should count honey as sugar. Honey has been used on wounds and burns since ancient times, and medical-grade honey is used in some wound dressings.[106]

History

Rock paintings in Spain about 8,000 years old show people taking honey from wild bees. The ancient Egyptians kept bees in clay pipes and used honey to sweeten cakes and to embalm the dead; Roman cooks mixed it with wine and vinegar, and mead, a drink of honey fermented with water, was brewed across Europe.[107]

Until sugar from cane became cheap in the 18th century, honey was the main sweetener in Europe, and large amounts of it were paid as rent and taxes.[108]

Production and trade

About 1.8 million tonnes of honey are produced each year. China is the largest producer, followed by Turkey, Iran and Argentina; Ukraine and New Zealand export large amounts of honey to Europe.[109]

Honey is one of the most often faked foods: cheap honey is sometimes mixed with sugar syrup made from rice or corn. Laboratories test for this by measuring the ratio of carbon isotopes in the sugars.[110]

Types

Monofloral honeys come mostly from one kind of flower and have their own colour and taste: acacia honey is pale and stays liquid, buckwheat honey is dark and strong, and manuka honey from New Zealand is sold at high prices for its supposed health effects.[111]

Creamed honey is honey that has been made to crystallise in a controlled way into very small crystals, so that it spreads like butter.[112]

In culture

Honey has a place in many religions: the Bible speaks of a land flowing with milk and honey, and in Judaism apples dipped in honey are eaten at the New Year for a sweet year ahead.[113]

Smartphone

A smartphone is a mobile phone that is also a small handheld computer, with a touchscreen, internet access and an operating system that can run downloaded apps.[114]

More than 1.2 billion smartphones are sold each year; most of them run Android or iOS.[115]

Hardware

Inside the case are a main circuit board carrying the processor, memory and radio chips, a lithium-ion battery, cameras, speakers and a vibration motor. The screen is a sandwich of toughened glass, a touch layer and an LCD or OLED panel.[116]

The case is usually aluminium, stainless steel, glass or plastic.[117]

Materials

A typical smartphone holds more than 60 elements. The battery uses lithium, cobalt and graphite; the circuit board copper, tin and tantalum; the screen indium tin oxide; and the speakers and vibration motor magnets of neodymium.[118]

Each phone contains small amounts of gold, silver and palladium in its connectors and chips, about 0.03 g of gold; recyclers recover these metals from large amounts of scrapped phones.[119]

Batteries

Smartphone batteries lose capacity with age and usually need replacing after two to three years. A swollen battery can catch fire and should be taken out of use at once.[120]

Environmental impact

Mining the metals needs large amounts of energy and water, and cobalt mining in particular has been linked to child labour. Fewer than one in five old phones is recycled.[121]

History

The first phones to combine a mobile phone with computer functions appeared in the 1990s. Touchscreen smartphones without a keyboard became common after 2007, and by 2013 more smartphones than basic phones were sold worldwide.[122]

Early smartphones were made with a removable battery and a plastic back; most phones made after about 2015 have a glued-in battery and a glass back that allows wireless charging.[123]

Software

The operating system manages the hardware and runs apps. Phones receive security updates for a limited number of years, after which they become less safe to use online.[124]

Repair

Screens and batteries are the parts that fail most often. A cracked screen can usually be replaced as one unit together with its digitizer; in many countries right-to-repair laws now require makers to sell spare parts and tools.[125]

Water damage is common: a phone that has been in water should be switched off at once and dried, and not charged until it is completely dry.[126]

pages.wikimed/Human_tooth:
Human tooth

Human teeth break down food by cutting and crushing it. An adult has 32 permanent teeth; a child has 20 milk (deciduous) teeth, which fall out between about 6 and 12 years of age.[127]

Structure

Each tooth has a crown above the gum and one or more roots set in the jaw bone. From the outside in, a tooth has three layers, enamel, dentine and pulp, and the root is covered with cementum.[128]

Enamel

Enamel is the hardest substance in the human body. It is about 96% mineral, mostly crystals of hydroxyapatite, a calcium phosphate, with the rest water and protein. Enamel has no living cells and cannot repair itself once it is lost.[129]

Dentine

Dentine, under the enamel, is about 70% mineral and is softer; it is full of tiny tubes, which is why exposed dentine is sensitive to cold.[130]

Pulp

The pulp in the centre holds the nerves and blood vessels.[131]

Decay

Bacteria in plaque turn sugar into acid, which dissolves the enamel. Sugary drinks between meals, which bathe the teeth in acid for long periods, do the most harm; brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and cutting down on sugar prevent most decay.[132]

Saliva neutralises the acid and contains large amounts of calcium and phosphate, which help early decay to harden again.[133]

Knocked-out teeth

A knocked-out adult tooth can often be saved if it is put back within an hour. Hold it by the crown, not the root, rinse it briefly if dirty, and push it back into the socket, or keep it in milk, and see a dentist at once. Never put a knocked-out milk tooth back.[134]

Development

Teeth begin to form in the jaw before birth. The first milk teeth appear at about six months, and the last permanent teeth, the wisdom teeth, usually come through between 17 and 25 years of age, if they do at all.[135]

Care

Brush for two minutes twice a day with a fluoride toothpaste, clean between the teeth, and see a dentist regularly. Children should be helped with brushing until they are about seven.[136]

A diet that contains large amounts of sugar, especially in drinks and sweets eaten between meals, is the main cause of decay in children.[137]

Other animals

Shark teeth are replaced throughout life, and the teeth of rodents grow all the time and are worn down by gnawing. Elephant tusks are incisor teeth made of dentine, which is the ivory of the trade.[138]

pages.wikipedia/Natural_gas:
Natural gas

Natural gas is a fossil fuel found underground, often together with oil, and burned for heating, cooking and to make electricity.[139]

It has no smell of its own; a sulfur compound, a mercaptan, is added so that leaks can be smelled.[140]

Composition

Raw natural gas is mostly methane, typically 70 to 90%, with ethane, propane and butane, and smaller shares of carbon dioxide, nitrogen and hydrogen sulfide. It is processed to remove water, hydrogen sulfide and most of the heavier hydrocarbons before it reaches homes.[141]

Uses

Power stations burn large amounts of natural gas to make electricity. Natural gas is also the main raw material for making ammonia for fertiliser.[142]

Safety

If you smell gas indoors, do not switch lights or appliances on or off, do not use a flame, open the doors and windows, leave the building, and call the gas emergency number from outside.[143]

Burning gas in a badly ventilated room or a faulty boiler produces carbon monoxide, which is invisible and deadly; a carbon monoxide alarm gives warning.[144]

Environment

Burning natural gas releases about half as much carbon dioxide as coal for the same energy. Methane that leaks unburned is a powerful greenhouse gas, and leaks of even small amounts of methane undo much of that advantage.[145]

History

Natural gas leaking from the ground and catching fire fed the eternal flames of ancient temples. Gas made from coal lit the streets of European cities in the 19th century; natural gas replaced it after the Second World War, when long pipelines were built.[146]

Transport

Most natural gas travels through pipelines. Across oceans it is shipped as liquefied natural gas (LNG), cooled to −162°C, at which it takes up 600 times less space.[147]

Large amounts of natural gas are stored underground in old gas fields and salt caverns so that more can be supplied in winter.[148]

Liquefied petroleum gas

Bottled gas for cooking, LPG, is not natural gas but a mixture of propane and butane, separated from natural gas or from oil. It is heavier than air, so a leak collects near the floor.[149]

pages.wikipedia/Peanut_butter:
Peanut butter

Peanut butter is a spread of ground, dry-roasted peanuts, eaten on bread or crackers and used in sauces and baking.[150]

Production

Peanuts are roasted, cooled, and their skins blown off. They are then ground into a paste between steel plates; the oil released by grinding makes the paste smooth.[151]

Most commercial peanut butter is 90% peanuts, with added salt, sugar and a stabiliser of hydrogenated vegetable oil, which stops the oil separating out. "Natural" peanut butter is only peanuts and sometimes salt, and needs stirring.[152]

Nutrition

Peanut butter contains large amounts of fat, mostly unsaturated, and about 25% protein; 100 g provides about 590 kilocalories.[153]

It is the main ingredient of ready-to-use therapeutic food, a paste of peanut butter, milk powder, sugar and vitamins used to treat children with severe malnutrition.[154]

Allergy

Peanut allergy is one of the most dangerous food allergies. Even small amounts of peanut can cause anaphylaxis in an allergic person, with swelling of the throat and difficulty breathing, which needs emergency treatment.[155]

History

The Aztecs and the Inca ground roasted peanuts into a paste. Modern peanut butter was patented in Canada in 1884 by Marcellus Edson, and was promoted in the United States around 1900 as a protein food for people who could not chew meat.[156]

Peanut butter sandwiches became a staple of American children during the Great Depression, when it was a cheap source of protein.[157]

Production

The United States, China and India grow most of the world's peanuts. American law requires anything sold as peanut butter to be at least 90% peanuts; spreads with less must be called peanut spread.[158]

Peanut butter is used in Southeast Asian satay sauce and West African groundnut stew, which is made with tomatoes, onions and chicken.[159]

pages.wikivoyage/Hoi_An:
Hoi An

Hoi An

Hoi An is a riverside town on the central coast of Vietnam, 30 km south of Da Nang, whose old trading port of wooden shophouses, Chinese assembly halls and lantern-lit lanes is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Understand

From the 16th to the 18th century Hoi An was one of the busiest ports of Southeast Asia, where Japanese, Chinese, Portuguese and Dutch merchants traded silk and porcelain. When the river silted up, trade moved to Da Nang and the town was left untouched, which is why it survived.

Today the Old Town is very touristy: nearly every shophouse is a tailor, a gallery, a cafe or a souvenir shop, and the lanes are packed in the evening. Early morning, before 08:00, is the best time to see it quietly.

Climate

The dry season is February to August, very hot from May. The rainy season, September to January, brings typhoons and floods: in October and November the river often floods the Old Town, and boats are rowed through the streets.

Festivals

On the 14th day of every lunar month the town turns off its electric lights for the Full Moon Lantern Festival, and people float paper lanterns with candles on the river. Tết, the Lunar New Year in January or February, closes many shops for a week.

Get in

The nearest airport is Da Nang International (DAD), 45 minutes by taxi or Grab for about VND 300,000. The nearest train station is also in Da Nang. Open-tour buses stop in Hoi An on the way between Hue and Nha Trang.

Get around

Cars and motorbikes are banned from the Old Town at most hours, so walk or cycle. Most hotels lend bicycles for free, and the 4 km ride to An Bang Beach through the rice fields is flat.

See

A ticket of VND 120,000, sold at booths at the edge of the Old Town, gives entry to five of the twenty-two heritage sites, among them the Japanese Covered Bridge, the old houses and the assembly halls.

Do

Have clothes made: hundreds of tailors can make a suit or a dress in 24 hours, from about USD 100. Choose the fabric carefully and allow time for two fittings.

Take a cooking class, which usually starts with a trip to the market, or a basket-boat ride in the coconut palm forest of Cam Thanh.

Eat

Cao lầu, thick noodles with pork, herbs and crispy croutons, is the town's own dish and is said to need water from one particular old well. Try also bánh mì from the stalls, and white rose dumplings.

Sleep

Homestays and guesthouses in the rice fields between the town and the beach cost USD 15 to 30; resorts line An Bang and Cua Dai beaches.

Stay safe

Hoi An is very safe. Watch for motorbikes when crossing roads outside the Old Town, and in the flood season follow local advice and keep away from the river banks.

Go next

  • My Son – Cham temple ruins in the jungle, an hour inland.
  • Da Nang – beaches and the Marble Mountains.

After a storm, flood or earthquake you may need to survive on your own for several days. Keep these supplies together in a bag or box that is easy to carry.

pages.wikipedia/Windmill:
Windmill

A windmill is a structure that converts wind power into rotational energy by means of vanes called sails or blades, traditionally to mill grain, pump water, or both.[160]

Windmills were used throughout the medieval and early modern periods; the horizontal or panemone windmill first appeared in Persia during the 9th century, and the vertical windmill first appeared in north-western Europe in the 12th century.[161]

History

Persia

The first practical windmills were panemone windmills, with sails that rotated in a horizontal plane around a vertical axis. They were built in the Sistan region of eastern Iran, where strong steady winds blow for 120 days each summer.[162]

Europe

Post mills

The earliest European windmills were post mills: the whole body of the mill, holding the machinery, turns on a single upright post to face the wind. The oldest known reference is from Yorkshire in 1185.[163]

Tower mills

In a tower mill only the cap at the top turns, carrying the sails; the body is a fixed brick or stone tower, which could be built much taller. Tower mills spread from the 13th century.[164]

Wind pumps

From the 1850s, small wind pumps with many metal blades were made in the United States to pump water from wells for cattle and homes on farms far from rivers. Over six million were built, and many still work.[165]

Operation

A miller turns the sails into the wind and sets the amount of sail cloth for the wind speed; too much sail in a strong wind can overspeed the mill and set it on fire from friction at the millstones.[166]

Modern use

Wind turbines, which make electricity, are the descendants of windmills. Small wind pumps are still used in Africa, Australia and the Americas where there is no electricity.[167]
