Valparaíso

Valparaíso

Valparaíso is a port city on the central coast of Chile, 120 km west of Santiago, built on forty-two steep hills around a wide bay.

Its tangle of painted houses, stairways and old funiculars made the historic quarter a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003, and it is the seat of the Chilean Congress.

Understand

History

Spanish sailors landed in the bay in 1536. For most of the 19th century Valparaíso was the first stop for ships coming round Cape Horn, and British, German and Italian merchants built banks, churches and mansions on the hills. The opening of the Panama Canal in 1914 took the ships away, and the city declined for most of the 20th century.

The heritage listing brought money back to the cerros Alegre and Concepción, which are now full of guesthouses and cafes, while much of the rest of the city remains poor.

Climate

The climate is mild and Mediterranean. Summer (December to March) is dry and sunny with highs of about 22°C, and is the best time to come. Winter (June to August) brings most of the year's rain and cool highs of 14°C. A morning sea fog, the camanchaca, is common at any time of year and usually burns off by noon.

Tourist information

The municipal tourist office has a kiosk at the foot of Muelle Prat and hands out a free map of the hills and the ascensores.

Get in

Most travellers arrive from Santiago, which is 90 minutes away by road.

By plane

The nearest international airport is Santiago's Arturo Merino Benítez (SCL), about 110 km away. Shared transfer vans go from the arrivals hall to any address in Valparaíso for about CLP 25,000 a person; the cheaper way is a Centropuerto bus to the Pajaritos stop in Santiago and a Valparaíso bus from there.

By bus

Turbus and Pullman buses leave Santiago's Terminal Alameda every 15 minutes from 06:00 to 22:00, take about 1 hour 45 minutes and cost CLP 4,000 to 6,000. They arrive at the Terminal Rodoviario on Avenida Pedro Montt, opposite the Congress.

By boat

Valparaíso is a stop for cruise ships between October and March; passengers are taken through the container port by shuttle to the Prat pier.

Get around

The flat strip along the bay, El Plan, is easy on foot. To reach the hills, use the ascensores, the colectivos, or the many stairways.

By ascensor

The ascensores are funicular lifts built between 1883 and 1916 to carry people up the hills. Eight still run, among them Concepción, Reina Victoria, El Peral and Artillería. A ride costs CLP 100 to 300, paid in coins at the top or bottom station. Ascensor Polanco is not a funicular but a true vertical lift reached through a tunnel.

By trolleybus

Valparaíso has one of the oldest trolleybus lines still running in the world, with buses from the 1940s and 1950s on Avenida Pedro Montt and Avenida Brasil. A ride costs about CLP 400.

By colectivo

Colectivos are shared taxis that run fixed routes up each hill; the number and destination are shown on the roof. They cost a little more than a bus and are the quickest way up to the cerros at night.

By metro

The Merval suburban train runs along the coast from Puerto station to Viña del Mar and on to Limache. You need a rechargeable card, sold at every station.

See

  • -33.04-71.621 La Sebastiana, Ferrari 692, Cerro Florida, ☎ +56 32 225 6606. Tu-Su 10:00-18:00. CLP 7,000. Pablo Neruda's house on the hill, five floors full of the poet's collections, with a view over the whole bay.edit
  • -33.04-71.622 Paseo Yugoslavo and Palacio Baburizza, Cerro Alegre. Tu-Su 10:30-18:30. CLP 6,000. An art nouveau mansion that holds the city's fine arts museum, at the top of Ascensor El Peral.edit
  • -33.04-71.623 Museo Marítimo Nacional, Paseo 21 de Mayo, Cerro Artillería. CLP 1,500. The naval museum, in the old naval school, has relics of the Battle of Iquique.edit
  • -33.04-71.624 Plaza Sotomayor. The main square, with the naval command building and the monument to the heroes of Iquique.edit

Do

Wander the hills: Cerro Alegre and Cerro Concepción are the most visited and are covered in murals. Free walking tours leave Plaza Sotomayor at 10:00 and 15:00; tip the guide at the end.

The Año Nuevo en el Mar fireworks on 31 December light the whole bay and are the largest in South America; up to a million people come, and every bed in the city is taken months ahead.

  • -33.04-71.625 Harbour boat tour, Muelle Prat. CLP 4,000. Small launches leave the pier for a 30-minute trip past the warships and the sea lions.edit

Buy

Chile uses the peso (CLP). ATMs (Redbanc) are on every street of El Plan but charge foreign cards a fee of about CLP 6,000 a withdrawal. Credit cards are accepted in most restaurants and hotels in the cerros; small shops, colectivos and the ascensores take cash only.

  • -33.04-71.626 Feria de Antigüedades, Avenida Argentina. Sa-Su. A large flea market of antiques, records and old tools.edit

Eat

Seafood is the thing to eat: try caldillo de congrio (conger eel soup), machas a la parmesana and empanadas de mariscos. The chorrillana, a mountain of chips under fried beef, onions and eggs, was invented in Valparaíso and is meant to be shared.

Budget

  • -33.04-71.627 Caleta Portales, Avenida España. CLP 3,000-8,000. The fishermen's cove on the road to Viña, with simple stalls frying the morning's catch.edit
  • -33.04-71.628 Mercado Cardonal, Avenida Uruguay. Upstairs from the vegetable market, cheap cocinerías serve set lunches.edit

Mid-range

  • -33.04-71.629 J. Cruz Malbrán, Condell 1466. The restaurant that claims to have invented the chorrillana, decorated with odds and ends from the last century.edit

Splurge

  • -33.04-71.6210 Café Turri, Templeman 147, Cerro Concepción. Fine seafood on a terrace at the top of Ascensor Concepción.edit

Drink

Bars cluster on Cerro Alegre and Cerro Concepción for a quiet drink with a view, and along Subida Ecuador and Avenida Errázuriz for loud clubs that open late, usually after midnight.

  • -33.04-71.6211 Bar La Playa, Serrano 567. An old sailors' bar from 1908, busy at weekends.edit

Sleep

Budget

  • -33.04-71.6212 Hostal Cerro Alegre, Urriola 562. dorms from CLP 12,000. A friendly hostel in an old house, with a kitchen and a roof terrace.edit
  • -33.04-71.6213 Casa Volante, Cerro Concepción. dorms from CLP 11,000. Clean, quiet and near the ascensor.edit

Mid-range

  • -33.04-71.6214 Hotel Brighton, Paseo Atkinson 151. doubles from CLP 60,000. A yellow wooden house hanging over the bay, with a bar on the balcony.edit

Splurge

  • -33.04-71.6215 Palacio Astoreca, Montealegre 149. doubles from CLP 200,000. A restored 1923 mansion with a spa.edit

Stay safe

Valparaíso has more street crime than most Chilean cities. Pickpockets work the buses, the ascensores and the crowds of Plaza Sotomayor and the Avenida Argentina market; keep phones and cameras out of sight.

The tourist hills are safe by day. After dark, stay on lit streets, avoid the stairways and the empty streets around the port, and take a colectivo or a taxi back up the hill rather than walking.

Stray dogs are everywhere and mostly harmless. In an emergency call 133 for the police (Carabineros) or 131 for an ambulance.

Stay healthy

Tap water is treated and safe to drink, though some visitors prefer bottled water for the taste. Summer sun is strong despite the cool breeze; use sunscreen.

Connect

Most cafes and guesthouses have free wifi. Prepaid SIM cards from Entel, Movistar and WOM are sold in the shops of Avenida Pedro Montt; bring your passport.

Go next

  • Viña del Mar – the beach resort next door, 15 minutes on the Merval train.
  • Casablanca Valley – white wine vineyards on the road to Santiago, with tastings.
  • Isla Negra – Neruda's third house, on the coast 80 km south.
pages.wikivoyage/Torres_del_Paine_National_Par:
Torres del Paine National Park

Torres del Paine National Park

Torres del Paine National Park is a national park in Chilean Patagonia, famous for the three granite towers that give it its name, its glaciers and its multi-day treks.

Understand

Landscape

The Paine massif rises straight out of the steppe to 3,050 m. The park also holds Grey Glacier, part of the Southern Patagonian Ice Field, and a chain of turquoise lakes fed by glacial melt.

Flora and fauna

Guanacos graze in large herds near the roads. Pumas live in the park and are seen more and more often, especially at dawn around Laguna Amarga. Condors circle the cliffs.

Climate

The weather changes by the hour. Summer (December to February) has the longest days and the most visitors, and the wind can exceed 100 km/h. Spring and autumn are quieter and colder; in winter many refugios close.

Get in

The park is 112 km north of Puerto Natales, the nearest town, which has an airport with flights from Santiago and Punta Arenas.

By bus

Buses leave Puerto Natales at 07:00 and 14:30 for Laguna Amarga, Pudeto and the park administration, taking about 2 hours. A return ticket costs about CLP 20,000.

By car

The road from Puerto Natales is paved as far as Cerro Castillo; after that it is gravel. Fuel is not sold in the park.

Fees and permits

All visitors must buy an entrance ticket online before arriving; tickets are not sold at the gates. The fee for foreign adults is CLP 49,000 for up to three days and CLP 74,000 for four days or more. Chilean residents pay less.

Camping is allowed only at the designated campsites, and every campsite and refugio on the W and O treks must be booked in advance. Rangers check reservations at each site.

Get around

A catamaran crosses Lago Pehoé from Pudeto to Paine Grande several times a day in summer, for CLP 30,000 one way. Otherwise you walk; there is no bus inside the park beyond the main road.

See

The towers themselves are best seen at sunrise from the Mirador Las Torres, a steep four-hour climb from the Welcome Center. Grey Glacier can be seen from a lookout near Refugio Grey or from a boat on Lago Grey.

Do

Hiking

The W trek takes four or five days and visits the towers, the French Valley and Grey Glacier. The O circuit adds the remote back side of the massif and the John Gardner Pass, and takes eight to ten days; it must be walked anticlockwise.

Kayaking

Guided kayak trips paddle among the icebergs below Grey Glacier.

Eat

The refugios sell meals and packed lunches at high prices, and their small shops stock pasta and snacks. Bring most of your food from Puerto Natales.

Sleep

Refugios

Refugios are mountain lodges with dorm beds, hot showers and meals. A bed costs USD 60 to 150 a night and must be booked months ahead for January.

Camping

Campsites with toilets cost USD 10 to 25 a person; a few free ranger campsites exist on the O circuit. Tents can be rented at most refugios.

Stay safe

The wind is the main danger: gusts can knock hikers over on exposed ridges, especially near Paine Grande. Fires are strictly forbidden after two huge wildfires started by visitors, in 2005 and 2011; stoves may be used only in marked cooking areas. Stay on the trails and carry layers for rain, wind and snow on the same day.

Go next

  • Puerto Natales – the base town, with gear rental and supermarkets.
  • El Calafate (Argentina) – for the Perito Moreno Glacier, five hours by bus.
pages.wikivoyage/Ollantaytambo:
Ollantaytambo

Ollantaytambo

Ollantaytambo is a small town in the Sacred Valley of Peru, at 2,800 m, with a great Inca fortress above it and the only rail station for Machu Picchu reachable by road.

Understand

The town keeps its Inca street plan and water channels, and people still live in Inca-built houses. Most visitors pass through on their way to Machu Picchu; staying a night or two helps with the altitude before the Inca Trail.

Get in

Colectivos from Cusco (Calle Pavitos) leave when full, take 90 minutes and cost PEN 15. Trains to Aguas Calientes, the town below Machu Picchu, leave from the station 1 km from the plaza; book with PeruRail or Inca Rail.

Get around

The town is tiny and everything is walkable. Mototaxis wait on the plaza for the station run.

See

The fortress terraces (part of the Boleto Turístico, PEN 70 for ten days) climb a steep hill above the plaza. Across the valley, the Inca storehouses of Pinkuylluna can be climbed for free.

Eat

Restaurants on the plaza serve alpaca, trout and quinoa soup. The market sells fruit and bread in the morning.

Sleep

Guesthouses near the plaza cost PEN 60 to 150 for a double; a few lodges near the station cost more.

Stay safe

The town is safe. Take it easy on the first day to avoid altitude sickness, drink plenty of water and avoid alcohol.

Go next

  • Machu Picchu – by train to Aguas Calientes, 90 minutes.
  • Pisac – for its market, an hour along the valley.
pages.wikivoyage/Venice:
Venice

Venice

Venice (Italian: Venezia) is a city of canals in north-eastern Italy, built on 118 small islands in a lagoon of the Adriatic Sea. It has no cars, and its palaces, churches and bridges draw more than 20 million people a year.

Understand

The city proper has about 50,000 residents, far fewer than its visitors on a summer day. It is divided into six districts (sestieri): Cannaregio, Castello, Dorsoduro, San Marco, San Polo and Santa Croce. Addresses use the sestiere and a house number, not the street name, so a map is essential.

Acqua alta

From October to January, high tides called acqua alta flood the lowest parts of the city, especially Piazza San Marco, for a few hours at a time. Sirens sound a few hours before; raised walkways are put out along the main routes, and shops sell plastic boots. Since 2020 the MOSE flood barriers have kept out most of the highest tides.

Climate

Summers are hot, humid and crowded, with mosquitoes in the evenings. Winters are cold and foggy but quiet. The busiest periods are Carnival (February), Easter and July to September; November and early December are the quietest.

Get in

By plane

Marco Polo Airport (VCE) is on the mainland 8 km north of the city. The Alilaguna water bus runs from the airport dock to San Marco in about 75 minutes for €15; ATVO buses go to Piazzale Roma in 20 minutes for €10. A water taxi costs around €120 for up to four people.

Treviso Airport (TSF), used by low-cost airlines, is 40 km away and linked by bus.

By train

Trains arrive at Venezia Santa Lucia station, on the Grand Canal at the north-west edge of the city. Make sure your train goes to Santa Lucia and not only to Venezia Mestre on the mainland. High-speed trains from Milan take 2 hours 25 minutes and from Rome about 4 hours.

By car

Cars can go no further than Piazzale Roma or the island of Tronchetto, where multi-storey car parks charge €25 to €40 a day. It is cheaper to park in Mestre and take the train or the tram across the bridge.

Day-tripper access fee

On about 30 busy days a year, between April and July, day visitors must pay an access fee of €5 to €10 to enter the old city between 08:30 and 16:00. It is paid online in advance; people staying overnight in the city are exempt but must still register for a QR code.

Get around

Venice is a city for walking, and getting lost is part of the experience. Signs painted on the walls point to San Marco, Rialto, the Ferrovia (station) and Piazzale Roma. Bicycles are not allowed in the city.

By vaporetto

The vaporetti, run by ACTV, are the city's buses. A single ticket is valid for 75 minutes and costs €9.50; passes for 1, 2, 3 or 7 days cost €25 to €65 and pay for themselves after three rides. Validate the ticket at the yellow reader on the pontoon before every ride. Line 1 runs slowly along the whole Grand Canal and is the cheapest way to see its palaces.

By traghetto

Traghetti are gondolas that ferry people across the Grand Canal at a few points where there is no bridge, for €2 a crossing.

By gondola

A gondola ride is the classic tourist experience and is not cheap: the official rate is €90 for 30 minutes during the day and €110 after 19:00, for up to five people. Agree the price and the route before you get in.

See

  • -33.04-71.6216 Basilica di San Marco, Piazza San Marco. daily 09:30-17:15. €3; Pala d'Oro extra. The cathedral, covered in gold mosaics. Bags must be left at the Ateneo San Basso; shoulders and knees must be covered.edit
  • -33.04-71.6217 Palazzo Ducale (Doge's Palace), Piazza San Marco 1. 09:00-18:00. €30 with the Museo Correr. The palace of the rulers of the republic, with the Bridge of Sighs leading to the prisons.edit
  • -33.04-71.6218 Gallerie dell'Accademia, Dorsoduro 1050. €15. Venetian painting from the 14th to the 18th century: Bellini, Titian, Tintoretto.edit
  • -33.04-71.6219 Rialto Bridge. The oldest of the four bridges over the Grand Canal, lined with shops.edit

Do

The Carnival of Venice is held for two weeks before Lent, in February, with masked balls and costumes in the streets. The Biennale art exhibition is held from April to November in odd-numbered years, and architecture in even years.

Take a vaporetto to the islands of the lagoon: Murano for glass-blowing, Burano for lace and coloured houses, and Torcello for its Byzantine cathedral.

Buy

The euro is used. Be wary of cheap "Murano" glass sold near San Marco; much of it is imported. Genuine Murano glass carries a trademark sticker.

Eat

Eating in Venice is expensive, and many restaurants near San Marco and Rialto serve poor food at high prices to people they will never see again. Walk a few streets away and look for a bacaro, a wine bar that serves cicchetti, small snacks eaten standing at the counter, for €1.50 to €3 each.

A cover charge (coperto) of €2 to €4 a person and sometimes a 12% service charge are added to restaurant bills; both should be shown on the menu.

Drink

The spritz, made with Aperol or Select, white wine and soda water, is the city's drink. Bars around Campo Santa Margherita in Dorsoduro are the liveliest at night.

Sleep

Hotels inside the old city are expensive, especially at weekends and during Carnival. Hotels in Mestre on the mainland cost about half as much and are 10 minutes by train.

Every hotel, B&B and rented flat in Venice charges a tourist tax (imposta di soggiorno) of €1 to €5 per person per night, depending on the season and the hotel's stars, for up to five nights; it is paid in cash at the hotel and is not usually included in booking prices.

Stay safe

Venice is very safe from violent crime. Pickpockets work the vaporetti, especially Line 1 and Line 2, and the crowds on the Rialto Bridge.

Fines for sitting on the steps of monuments, swimming in the canals, eating on the steps or walking in swimwear are enforced by the municipal police and can reach €500.

Go next

  • Padua – 30 minutes by train, with Giotto's chapel.
  • Verona – 70 minutes by train.
  • Lido – the beach island, by vaporetto.
pages.wikivoyage/Luxor:
Luxor

Luxor

Luxor is a city on the east bank of the Nile in Upper Egypt, on the site of ancient Thebes. With the temples of Karnak and Luxor on the east bank and the royal tombs on the west, it holds more ancient monuments than anywhere else in Egypt.

Understand

The city is divided by the Nile: the modern town, the railway station and most hotels are on the East Bank, and the Valley of the Kings, the Valley of the Queens and the mortuary temples are on the West Bank. Summer temperatures pass 40°C from May to September, so the main tourist season runs from October to April, peaking at Christmas.

Tickets

Each site has its own ticket office, and tickets are sold only at the office at the entrance of each site or, for the West Bank, partly at the central ticket office near the Colossi of Memnon. Prices are in Egyptian pounds and rise most years. Students with an ISIC card pay half. Cards are accepted at the larger sites, but carry cash for the smaller ones.

The Luxor Pass, sold at the Karnak and Valley of the Kings ticket offices, covers almost every site for five days and costs USD 100 for foreigners (USD 50 for students); bring a passport photo.

Get in

By plane

Luxor International Airport (LXR) is 7 km east of town, with flights from Cairo (1 hour) and charter flights from Europe. A taxi to the town costs EGP 150 to 250; agree the price before you get in.

By train

Sleeper trains from Cairo leave Giza station every evening and arrive in Luxor about ten hours later. Day trains are cheaper and slower. The station is in the centre of the East Bank, 10 minutes' walk from Luxor Temple.

By boat

Nile cruise boats sail between Luxor and Aswan in three to five days, stopping at Edfu and Kom Ombo.

Get around

The East Bank sights are close enough to walk between or to reach by horse-drawn carriage (calèche). Agree a price for the whole trip, and insist on a well-treated horse.

To cross to the West Bank, take the public ferry from the dock opposite Luxor Temple for EGP 10, or a motorboat for a little more. On the West Bank, hire a taxi for the day, rent a bicycle, or join a tour.

See

East Bank

  • -33.04-71.6220 Karnak Temple, 3 km north of the centre. 06:00-17:30. The largest temple complex of ancient Egypt, with the Great Hypostyle Hall of 134 columns.edit
  • -33.04-71.6221 Luxor Temple, Corniche el-Nil. 06:00-22:00. Lit up at night, and best visited after sunset when it is cool.edit

West Bank

  • -33.04-71.6222 Valley of the Kings. 06:00-17:00. The tombs of the New Kingdom pharaohs. The general ticket includes three tombs; the tombs of Tutankhamun, Seti I and Ramses VI need extra tickets. Photography is allowed only with a photo ticket.edit
  • -33.04-71.6223 Medinet Habu. The mortuary temple of Ramses III, with deep, well-preserved carvings and few crowds.edit
  • -33.04-71.6224 Colossi of Memnon. Two seated statues of Amenhotep III, 18 m high, free to see from the road.edit

Visiting hours at most West Bank sites are 06:00 to 17:00 in winter, and the tombs close an hour earlier in summer. Go as early as you can to avoid the heat and the tour groups.

Do

A hot-air balloon flight over the West Bank at sunrise costs USD 50 to 150. Choose a company with a good safety record; there have been fatal accidents.

Buy

Bargaining is expected in the souq and with calèche drivers. Start at a third of the first price.

Eat

Try koshary, fuul and ta'meyya from street stands, and stuffed pigeon in the restaurants on the West Bank.

Sleep

Large hotels line the Corniche on the East Bank; quieter guesthouses are found on the West Bank, some with views of the hills.

Stay safe

Luxor is safe for visitors, but touts and hassle are constant: drivers, guides, boatmen and shopkeepers will follow you down the street. A firm "la, shukran" (no, thank you) helps.

The Tourist Police, in white uniforms in summer and black in winter, have posts at every major site and at the station, and their officers speak some English; go to them if you are cheated or robbed. The ordinary police can be reached on 122.

Drink plenty of water in the heat; heatstroke is a real risk at the West Bank sites, where there is little shade.

Go next

  • Aswan – 3 hours south by train.
  • Dendera – the Temple of Hathor, an hour north by taxi.
pages.wikivoyage/Yellowstone_National_Park:
Yellowstone National Park

Yellowstone National Park

Yellowstone National Park is the oldest national park in the United States, established in 1872, covering 8,983 km² mostly in the northwest corner of Wyoming. It sits on a supervolcano and holds half the world's geysers.

Understand

The park is a high plateau, mostly above 2,000 m. Snow can fall in any month, and most roads are closed to cars from early November to late April. About 4 million people come each year, most of them in July and August.

Visitor centers

The park has several visitor centers, open from spring to autumn, with exhibits, maps and ranger talks. The Old Faithful Visitor Education Center shows predicted eruption times for the main geysers. Albright Visitor Center at Mammoth Hot Springs is the only one open all year.

Get in

There are five entrances: North (Gardiner, Montana), Northeast, East, South and West (West Yellowstone, Montana). Only the North Entrance road is open to cars all year.

By plane

The closest airports are Yellowstone Airport in West Yellowstone (summer only), Bozeman (BZN), 90 miles from the North Entrance, and Jackson Hole (JAC), 50 miles south of the South Entrance.

By car

Most people drive. Rental cars are available at all the airports, and it is worth booking months ahead for summer.

Fees and permits

A private vehicle pass costs $35 and is valid for seven days; the America the Beautiful annual pass, $80, covers every national park. Backcountry camping and fishing need separate permits from a ranger station.

Get around

The Grand Loop Road, 142 miles long, connects the main sights in a figure eight. Speed limits are 45 mph or lower, and traffic stops often for bison on the road, so allow far more time than the distances suggest. There is no public transport inside the park.

See

Old Faithful erupts about every 90 minutes. The Grand Prismatic Spring, the largest hot spring in the country, is best seen from the overlook on the Fairy Falls trail. The Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone has two waterfalls, the Upper and Lower Falls.

Bison, elk and pronghorn are common in the Lamar and Hayden valleys, where wolves and grizzly bears are often seen at dawn and dusk through a telescope.

Do

There are more than 900 miles of hiking trails. In winter, snowcoach and snowmobile tours run to Old Faithful.

Eat

Restaurants and cafeterias are found at Old Faithful, Canyon, Lake and Mammoth, and general stores sell groceries. Picnic areas are spread along the roads.

Sleep

The park has nine lodges, among them the Old Faithful Inn, and twelve campgrounds. Lodges and the reservable campgrounds fill up a year in advance for July; gateway towns such as West Yellowstone and Gardiner have many more motels.

Stay safe

Stay at least 25 yards from all wildlife and 100 yards from bears and wolves. Bison injure more visitors than any other animal; they look slow but run at 35 mph. Carry bear spray on the trails, make noise, and hike in groups.

Stay on boardwalks in the geyser basins: the ground is thin crust over boiling water, and people have died after stepping or falling into hot springs. Swimming in thermal features is illegal.

Go next

  • Grand Teton National Park – directly south.
  • Cody – 50 miles east, with a rodeo every summer night.
pages.wikivoyage/Laos:
Laos

Laos

Laos is a landlocked country in Southeast Asia, bordered by Thailand, Myanmar, China, Vietnam and Cambodia. It is the least crowded and most relaxed country of the region, a land of mountains, rivers, Buddhist temples and slow boats.

Understand

History

The kingdom of Lan Xang, the "land of a million elephants", was founded in 1353 and was one of the largest states of Southeast Asia. It split into three kingdoms in the 18th century, fell under Siamese rule, and became part of French Indochina in 1893. During the Vietnam War the United States dropped more than two million tons of bombs on Laos, more than on all of Europe in the Second World War. The communist Pathet Lao took power in 1975 and still governs.

People

About half of the 7.5 million people are ethnic Lao; the rest belong to more than forty other groups, among them the Hmong and the Khmu in the mountains. Most Lao are Theravada Buddhists, and every village has its temple (wat).

Climate

The dry season runs from November to April. November to February is cool and pleasant and the best time to visit; March and April are very hot and smoky from the burning of fields. The rainy season, May to October, brings afternoon downpours, green landscapes and muddy roads, and some rural roads become impassable.

Holidays

Pi Mai, the Lao New Year, is celebrated from 14 to 16 April with three days of water throwing; expect to be soaked, and keep phones in a plastic bag. Boun Ok Phansa, at the end of Buddhist Lent in October, is marked with boat races on the Mekong and floating candles.

Regions

  • Northern Laos – mountains, hill tribes and Luang Prabang.
  • Central Laos – the capital Vientiane and the karst country of Vang Vieng and Thakhek.
  • Southern Laos – the Bolaven Plateau, Wat Phou and the Four Thousand Islands.

Get in

Visa

Most nationalities can get a 30-day visa on arrival at the international airports and the main land borders for USD 30 to 42, depending on nationality; bring a passport photo and US dollars in cash. An e-visa is also available online and is accepted at the airports and at the Friendship Bridge.

By plane

Wattay International Airport in Vientiane and Luang Prabang International Airport have flights from Bangkok, Hanoi, Kunming and Singapore. Taxis from Wattay to central Vientiane cost a fixed KIP 100,000.

By train

The Laos–China Railway, opened in 2021, links Vientiane with Luang Prabang, Vang Vieng and the Chinese border at Boten; international trains continue to Kunming. Tickets sell out days ahead and must be bought with your passport at a station or through the LCR app. A train from Thailand crosses the Friendship Bridge from Nong Khai to Khamsavath station near Vientiane.

By land

The busiest border is the First Thai–Lao Friendship Bridge between Nong Khai and Vientiane. Buses from Hanoi and Danang cross into Laos at several passes, but the journeys are long, often twenty hours or more.

By boat

The slow boat from Huay Xai on the Thai border down the Mekong to Luang Prabang takes two days, with a night in the village of Pakbeng.

Get around

By train

The new railway has made the trip from Vientiane to Luang Prabang a two-hour ride; by road it takes nine hours or more.

By bus

Buses and minibuses link all the towns, but roads in the mountains are narrow and winding, and travel sickness is common. VIP buses have reclining seats on the main routes; local buses stop wherever they are waved down.

By songthaew and tuk-tuk

Songthaews, pickup trucks with two benches in the back, are the local transport between villages. In towns tuk-tuks charge KIP 20,000 to 50,000 for a short trip; agree the price first.

By motorbike

Renting a motorbike costs about KIP 150,000 a day. Many travellers do the Thakhek Loop, a four-day ride through caves and karst. You need a valid licence for motorbikes from home and an International Driving Permit to be insured, and a helmet; accidents are common.

Talk

Lao is the official language and is close to Thai; many Lao understand Thai from television. English is spoken in the tourist centres, and older people sometimes speak French.

See

Luang Prabang, a UNESCO town of temples and French villas, is the highlight of most trips. The Plain of Jars near Phonsavan holds thousands of stone jars about 2,000 years old, scattered over the hills. Wat Phou is a Khmer temple older than Angkor Wat.

Do

Tubing and kayaking on the Nam Song at Vang Vieng, trekking to hill-tribe villages from Luang Namtha, and cycling round the islands of Si Phan Don are the most popular activities.

Buy

Money

The currency is the kip (LAK). Thai baht and US dollars are also taken in tourist areas, but at poor rates. ATMs are found in all towns but charge KIP 20,000 to 40,000 a withdrawal and give at most KIP 1–2 million at a time. Credit cards are accepted only in larger hotels and some restaurants.

Costs

Laos is cheap: a budget traveller can manage on USD 25 a day, and a bowl of noodle soup costs KIP 30,000.

Bargaining

Bargaining is normal in markets but is done gently; the night market in Luang Prabang is relaxed by Asian standards.

Eat

Sticky rice (khao niao), eaten with the fingers from a small basket, comes with every meal. Larb, a salad of minced meat or fish with herbs and lime, is the national dish. French baguettes (khao jee) are sold everywhere for breakfast, a legacy of the colonial years.

Drink

Beerlao is the national beer and is excellent. Lao-lao is a strong rice spirit offered in villages. Bars in the towns must close by 23:30 by law, though some stay open later.

Sleep

Guesthouses cost USD 8 to 20 for a double in most towns; Luang Prabang and Vientiane also have boutique hotels in old houses. Homestays are possible in many villages, often arranged through trekking companies.

Stay safe

Unexploded ordnance

Millions of bombs dropped during the Vietnam War did not explode, and they still kill and injure people every year, especially in the provinces of Xieng Khouang, Savannakhet and Saravan. Never leave marked paths in the countryside, never touch metal objects, and at the Plain of Jars stay between the white and red markers.

Crime

Violent crime against visitors is rare, but bag snatching from motorbikes happens in Vientiane and Vang Vieng. Drug laws are strict and the police sometimes target backpackers.

Roads

Roads are the biggest danger: drive slowly, avoid riding at night, and wear a helmet.

Stay healthy

Malaria is a risk in rural areas, especially in the south, but not in Vientiane or Luang Prabang; ask a travel clinic before you go whether you need tablets. Dengue fever is common in the rainy season; use repellent during the day as well. Do not drink tap water; bottled and filtered water is sold everywhere, and many guesthouses refill bottles. Medical care is poor outside Vientiane, and serious cases are taken across the bridge to hospitals in Udon Thani in Thailand.

Respect

Dress modestly at temples, covering shoulders and knees, and take off your shoes before going inside a house or a temple building. Women must not touch monks or hand things to them directly. Pointing with the feet and touching anyone's head are rude.

Connect

Prepaid SIM cards from Unitel and Lao Telecom are cheap and sold at the airports; bring your passport. Mobile data is good in towns but patchy in the mountains.

Go next

From the south, the border crossing at Nong Nok Khiene leads to Stung Treng in Cambodia; from the north, the slow boat or the bus returns to Chiang Khong in Thailand.
pages.wikivoyage/Cold_weather:
Cold weather

Cold weather can be dangerous for the unprepared traveller, but with the right clothes and habits a winter trip to the Arctic, the mountains or a continental city can be safe and comfortable.

Understand

The body loses heat by contact with cold ground, by wind, by wet clothes and by breathing. Wind makes cold much worse: at −10°C a wind of 30 km/h feels like −20°C, and bare skin can freeze in under 30 minutes at a wind chill of −28°C.

Get around

Driving on snow and ice needs winter tyres, which are compulsory in many countries in winter. Carry a shovel, a blanket, warm clothes and food in the car, and tell someone your route. If you get stuck, stay with the car: it is easier to find than a person.

Eat

Eat more than usual. Fat and carbohydrate keep the body warm, and a snack before sleeping helps you stay warm through the night.

Drink

Cold air is dry and you lose a lot of water by breathing, so drink plenty even when you are not thirsty. Alcohol makes you feel warm but makes the body lose heat faster; avoid it outdoors.

Sleep

A sleeping bag is only as warm as the mat under it: use a thick insulating mat, or two. Change into dry clothes before getting into the bag and wear a hat.

Stay safe

Clothing

Dress in layers: a base layer that moves sweat away from the skin (wool or synthetic, never cotton), a warm middle layer such as fleece or down, and a windproof and waterproof shell. Cover the head, hands and feet; mittens are warmer than gloves.

Frostbite

Frostbite usually affects the fingers, toes, nose, ears and cheeks. The skin first turns red and stings, then goes white or greyish-yellow, hard and numb. Warm the area gently with body heat; do not rub it with snow and do not use direct heat such as a fire or a heater, which burns numb skin. Get medical help for anything more than the mildest frostbite.

Hypothermia

Hypothermia is a fall in the body's core temperature. Signs are shivering, clumsiness, slurred speech and confusion; when the shivering stops the person is in serious danger. Get them out of the wind and wet, replace wet clothes with dry ones, wrap them in blankets including the head, give warm sweet drinks if they are fully awake, and call emergency services.

Stay healthy

Snow reflects up to 80% of the sun's ultraviolet light, so snow blindness and sunburn are real risks: wear sunglasses or goggles and sunscreen even on cloudy days.

pages.wikivoyage/Salkantay_Trek:
Salkantay Trek

Salkantay Trek

The Salkantay Trek is a five-day trek in the Andes of Peru from Mollepata to Aguas Calientes, below Machu Picchu, crossing a 4,600 m pass beside the snow-capped Salkantay mountain. Unlike the Inca Trail, it needs no permit.

Understand

The route climbs from farmland to glaciers and down into cloud forest and coffee farms in five days, covering about 72 km. The pass is cold and often snowy; the lower valleys are hot and full of biting sandflies.

Prepare

No permit is needed and the trek can be walked without a guide, but most people join a group tour from Cusco, which includes mules, cooks and tents and costs USD 250 to 600. The first step for independent hikers is to spend at least two or three days in Cusco to get used to the altitude before starting. A Machu Picchu entry ticket must be bought in advance online; tickets for the end of the trek sell out weeks ahead in the dry season.

Bring warm layers and a sleeping bag rated to −10°C, rain gear, insect repellent and cash in soles for the villages.

Get in

Colectivos to Mollepata leave Cusco from Calle Arcopata at 05:00 and take about three hours. Tour groups are collected from their hotels before dawn.

Go

Day 1: Mollepata to Soraypampa, 4 hours, climbing to 3,900 m. In the afternoon walk up to Humantay Lake, a turquoise glacier lake at 4,200 m.

Day 2: Soraypampa over the Salkantay Pass (4,600 m) to Chaullay, the hardest day, about 22 km and 9 hours. Start before dawn to cross the pass in the calm morning.

Day 3: Chaullay down the Santa Teresa valley to La Playa, an easy day through cloud forest with orchids and passion fruit.

Day 4: La Playa over an Inca path to Llactapata, with the first view of Machu Picchu across the valley, and down to the Hidroeléctrica station.

Day 5: Walk along the railway to Aguas Calientes, 11 km and 3 hours, or take the train; the next morning visit Machu Picchu.

Stay safe

Altitude sickness is the main danger on the first two days: headache, nausea and breathlessness are common at the pass. If symptoms get worse, go down; do not cross the pass with a severe headache or confusion.

The weather on the pass can turn to snow in an hour. Do not walk the pass alone in the rainy season (December to March), when landslides close parts of the lower trail.

Go next

  • Machu Picchu
  • Cusco – by train from Aguas Calientes to Ollantaytambo and bus on.
pages.wikivoyage/Quechua_phrasebook:
Quechua phrasebook

Quechua (Runasimi) is the most widely spoken indigenous language of the Americas, with about 8 million speakers in Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador. It was the language of the Inca Empire.

Understand

There are many dialects; this phrasebook uses the Southern Quechua of Cusco. Quechua builds words by adding suffixes to a root, so one long word can say what English says in a sentence.

Pronunciation guide

Quechua has only three vowels, a, i and u; e and o are heard only next to q. The letter q is pronounced far back in the throat. An apostrophe after a consonant (as in ch'aki, dry) marks a popped, ejective sound.

Phrase list

Basics

  • Hello: Allillanchu? (literally, "are you well?")
  • Thank you: Sulpayki or Yusulpayki
  • Yes: Arí. No: Mana.
  • How much is it?: Hayk'a chaninmi?
  • Where is the toilet?: Maypitaq baño?

Getting around

  • Where is the bus going?: Maymantaq kay carro rin?
  • Stop here, please: Kaypi sayay, ama hina kaspa.

Eating

  • Water: Yaku
  • Potato: Papa
  • Delicious!: Ancha misk'i!

Learning more

Quechua is taught at language schools in Cusco and at the university.
